Explain the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK) framework: 5 Process Groups (Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring & Controlling, Closing) and 10 Knowledge Areas with their interactions throughout project lifecycle.
questions.solutionOutline: PMBOK organizes project activities. 5 Process Groups span lifecycle from initial charter authorization to final handover. 10 Knowledge Areas: Integration, Scope, Schedule, Cost, Quality, Resource, Communications, Risk, Procurement, and Stakeholder Management. Matrix maps 49 individual processes across groups and areas.

questions.text: Explain Project Scope Management. How is the Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) constructed? Explain the 100% Rule, WBS Dictionary, and Scope Baseline control against Scope Creep.
questions.solutionOutline: Defines and controls what is and is not included in project. WBS decomposes total project scope hierarchically into smaller, manageable work packages. 100% Rule: WBS includes 100% of work defined by project scope without omitting or adding unauthorized tasks. WBS Dictionary provides detailed descriptions of work packages. Scope baseline (Scope Statement, WBS, WBS Dictionary) prevents uncontrolled scope creep via formal change control.

questions.text: Construct a Project Network Diagram using the Precedence Diagramming Method (PDM). Given activity dependencies and durations, determine Early Start (ES), Early Finish (EF), Late Start (LS), Late Finish (LF), Total Float (TF), Free Float (FF), and the Critical Path.
questions.solutionOutline: PDM uses activity-on-node (AON) representation. Forward pass calculates earliest start and finish: EF = ES + Duration. Backward pass calculates latest start and finish: LS = LF - Duration. Total Float TF = LS - ES = LF - EF (time activity can be delayed without delaying project completion). Free Float FF = min(ES of successors) - EF. Critical path is longest path where Total Float = 0.

questions.text: Explain Program Evaluation and Review Technique (PERT). Derive formulas for expected activity duration $t_e = \frac{a + 4m + b}{6}$ and variance $\sigma^2 = \left(\frac{b - a}{6}\right)^2$. Calculate the probability of project completion before a target deadline using standard normal $Z$-tables.
questions.solutionOutline: Probabilistic scheduling method accounting for uncertainty using beta distribution. Estimates: Optimistic time a, Most likely time m, Pessimistic time b. Total expected project duration T_e = sum(t_e on critical path); total variance sigma_p^2 = sum(sigma^2 on critical path). Compute standard normal deviate Z = (Target Date - T_e) / sigma_p, lookup cumulative probability P(T <= Target).

questions.text: Explain Project Schedule Compression techniques: Crashing and Fast-Tracking. Given normal time, normal cost, crash time, and crash cost, determine optimal crashing sequence to compress schedule at minimum additional cost.
questions.solutionOutline: Techniques to shorten schedule without altering project scope. Fast-tracking executes sequential activities in parallel (increases risk and rework). Crashing adds resources to critical activities to compress duration. Crash cost slope = (Crash Cost - Normal Cost) / (Normal Time - Crash Time). Iteratively crash critical activities with lowest cost slope until desired duration is reached or activities become non-critical.

questions.text: Explain Earned Value Management (EVM). Define Planned Value (PV), Earned Value (EV), and Actual Cost (AC). Derive Cost Variance (CV), Schedule Variance (SV), Cost Performance Index (CPI), Schedule Performance Index (SPI), and Estimate at Completion (EAC).
questions.solutionOutline: Integrates scope, schedule, and cost. PV = budgeted cost of work scheduled. EV = budgeted cost of work actually performed. AC = actual cost incurred. CV = EV - AC (>0 under budget). SV = EV - PV (>0 ahead of schedule). CPI = EV / AC (>1 good). SPI = EV / PV (>1 good). Estimate at Completion EAC = BAC / CPI (assuming present cost performance continues).

questions.text: Explain Project Risk Management processes: Risk Identification, Qualitative Risk Analysis (Probability-Impact Matrix), Quantitative Risk Analysis (Decision Tree Analysis / EMV), and Risk Response Strategies (Avoid, Transfer, Mitigate, Accept).
questions.solutionOutline: Identifies and manages uncertainties. Qualitative analysis scores probability (1-5) and impact (1-5) to rank risks on P-I matrix. Quantitative analysis computes Expected Monetary Value EMV = Probability * Financial Impact using decision trees. Responses for negative threats: Avoid (eliminate cause), Transfer (insurance/subcontracting), Mitigate (reduce probability/impact), Accept (establish contingency reserve).

questions.text: Explain Project Stakeholder Management. Describe Stakeholder Identification, Power-Interest Grid ($2 \times 2$ matrix), and Stakeholder Engagement Assessment Matrix.
questions.solutionOutline: Identifies individuals/organizations affected by project. Power-Interest Grid classifies stakeholders into 4 quadrants: High Power / High Interest (Manage Closely - key decision makers); High Power / Low Interest (Keep Satisfied); Low Power / High Interest (Keep Informed); Low Power / Low Interest (Monitor). Stakeholder engagement matrix compares current vs desired engagement levels (Unaware, Resistant, Neutral, Supportive, Leading).

questions.text: Explain Project Human Resource Management. Describe Tuckman's Team Development Stages (Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing, Adjourning), RACI Responsibility Assignment Matrix, and Conflict Management techniques.
questions.solutionOutline: Tuckman stages: Forming (orientation), Storming (interpersonal friction/competition), Norming (cohesion and shared standards), Performing (high productivity), Adjourning (project completion and dissolution). RACI matrix defines who is Responsible, Accountable (only one per task), Consulted, and Informed. Conflict management strategies: Collaborate/Problem-Solve (win-win), Compromise, Smooth/Accommodate, Force/Direct, Withdraw/Avoid.

questions.text: Explain Project Procurement Management. Compare Contract Types: Fixed-Price Contracts (FP/FFP), Cost-Reimbursable Contracts (CPFF/CPIF), and Time & Materials Contracts (T&M) from buyer and seller risk perspectives.
questions.solutionOutline: Procuring goods and services from external vendors. Fixed Price: set price for well-defined deliverables; highest risk to seller, lowest to buyer. Cost Reimbursable: buyer pays actual costs plus contractor fee/profit; highest risk to buyer, lowest to seller (used when scope uncertain). Time and Materials: hybrid contract paid on hourly rates plus materials, used for staff augmentation or short-term expert consultancies.

questions.text: Describe the Project Charter: key components, project justification, measurable objectives, high-level requirements, and authorization of the project manager.
questions.solutionOutline: Formal document issued by project sponsor or initiator authorizing project existence. Provides PM with authority to apply organizational resources to project activities. Components: Business need/justification, measurable objectives and success criteria, high-level requirements, summary milestone schedule, pre-approved budget, assigned project manager authority, sponsor signature.

questions.text: Explain Agile and DevOps Trends in ICT Project Management. Contrast Traditional Waterfall project management with Agile frameworks (Scrum, Kanban) in terms of scope flexibility, iteration cadence, and continuous delivery pipelines.
questions.solutionOutline: Traditional Waterfall uses rigid sequential phases with upfront planning and strict change requests. Agile promotes iterative 2-4 week sprints, continuous customer feedback, and emergent architecture. Kanban focuses on continuous flow with WIP limits. DevOps unifies software development and IT operations via automated CI/CD deployment pipelines, automated testing, and infrastructure-as-code.

questions.text: Explain Project Communication Management. Calculate the number of potential communication channels $C = \frac{N(N-1)}{2}$ for a team of $N$ stakeholders. Explain communication models, barriers, and communication management plans.
questions.solutionOutline: Ensures timely and appropriate collection, distribution, and storage of project information. Communication channels grow quadratically: N=10 gives 45 channels; N=20 gives 190 channels, illustrating communication complexity. Communication management plan specifies who needs what information, format, frequency, distribution channel, and responsible person.

questions.text: Explain Project Quality Management. Describe Plan Quality, Quality Assurance, and Quality Control. Explain the 7 Basic Quality Tools (Fishbone/Ishikawa diagram, Pareto chart, Control charts, Checklists, Histograms, Scatter diagrams, Flowcharts).
questions.solutionOutline: Plan Quality identifies standards; QA audits quality requirements and process results; QC monitors deliverables to eliminate defects. 7 QC tools: Cause-and-Effect (Fishbone) identifies root causes; Pareto chart (80/20 rule) highlights vital few defects; Control charts monitor process stability between Upper/Lower Control Limits; Checklists ensure consistency; Histograms show distributions; Scatter plots identify correlations; Flowcharts map processes.
